Across inland New South Wales and Victoria, a run of two or three months with almost nothing is ordinary. So the tank has to hold enough to bridge the gap, not enough to hold the year's rain. A household using 240 litres a day needs about 21,600 litres to cover ninety days, which is why 22,500 litre tanks are so common on rural blocks.

## Rainfall varies more than the average suggests

The annual average for a place like Wagga or Wodonga hides a lot. Some years come in well under, and the dry years are exactly the years the tank matters. If the number above is close, size up, because the cost of a bigger tank is small next to the cost of carting water.

Your local council or the Bureau of Meteorology has the long term figures for your postcode, and the median is a more useful number than the mean for this purpose.

## What this does not cover

Drinking water quality, first flush and filtration, pump sizing, and whether a tank is required or subsidised where you are. Requirements differ between New South Wales and Victoria and between councils, and new builds are often covered by separate rules again.

faqs.q: How much rainwater can I collect from my roof?
faqs.a: One millimetre of rain on one square metre of roof is one litre. Multiply your roof footprint in square metres by the annual rainfall in millimetres, then take off about fifteen per cent for first flush, overflow and evaporation. A 200 square metre roof under 600mm collects roughly 102,000 litres a year.

faqs.q: Do I use the roof area or the roof footprint?
faqs.a: The footprint, which is the outline of the roof seen from above. Rain falls vertically, so a steep roof catches no more water than a flat one covering the same ground. Only count the sections that actually drain to the tank.

faqs.q: What size rainwater tank do I need?
faqs.a: Size it to bridge the dry spell rather than to hold the year's rainfall. Inland New South Wales and Victoria regularly go two or three months with almost nothing, so a household using 240 litres a day needs somewhere near 21,600 litres to cover ninety days. That is why 22,500 litre tanks are so common on rural blocks.

faqs.q: Is the annual average rainfall a safe number to plan on?
faqs.a: Not on its own. The average hides considerable variation, and the dry years are precisely the years the tank matters. If the calculation comes out close to your usage, size up. The Bureau of Meteorology holds long term figures by location, and the median is more useful than the mean here.

title: Firewood calculator
description: Work out the real cost per cubic metre of a firewood load from the stacked measurements, compare sellers honestly, and see how long it will last.
standfirst: Stack measurements and price in, cost per cubic metre out.
body:
Firewood is the last thing many people buy without a unit. A trailer load, a ute load and a six by four are not measurements, and comparing two sellers who use them is guesswork. Stack it, measure it, and you have a number that means something.

## The sum

Stacked volume is length times height times depth. A stack 2.4 metres long, 1.2 high and half a metre deep is 1.44 cubic metres. At $380 that is about $264 a cubic metre, and that is the figure to compare sellers on.

## Stacked and loose are different volumes

The same wood tipped in a heap measures roughly a third more than it does stacked, because you are measuring the air between the pieces. A seller quoting loose cubic metres and a seller quoting stacked cubic metres are not quoting the same thing, and the gap is large enough to reverse which one is cheaper.

If you are quoted a volume, ask whether it is stacked or loose. If wood is tipped in your driveway, stack it before you judge it.

## Seasoning matters more than species

Wet wood is the most expensive firewood there is. Water in the timber has to be boiled off before the wood will burn properly, and that energy comes out of your heating rather than going into the room. Green or unseasoned wood also builds creosote in the flue, which is a chimney fire risk rather than an inconvenience.

Seasoned wood is lighter than it looks, has checking cracks across the end grain, and knocks together with a sharp sound instead of a dull one. If it hisses at the ends when it burns, it was not ready.

## Your rights

In both New South Wales and Victoria, firewood is sold by volume and a seller should be able to tell you the quantity you are getting and give you a receipt showing it. If a seller cannot or will not state a volume, that is the answer to whether to buy from them.

There are also rules about where firewood may be taken from. Commercial firewood must come from authorised sources, and collecting from roadsides, reserves and public land is restricted in both states. Ask where it came from.

## Buy in summer

Firewood is cheapest and driest at the end of summer and dearest in the middle of a cold snap when everyone has run out at once. A season ahead is the cheapest firewood you will ever burn, and it will be properly dry by the time you need it.

faqs.q: How do I know if a firewood load is good value?
faqs.a: Stack it, measure length by height by depth for the volume in cubic metres, and divide the price by that. Cost per stacked cubic metre is the only figure that lets you compare two sellers. A trailer load or a ute load is not a unit of measurement.

faqs.q: What is the difference between stacked and loose cubic metres?
faqs.a: The same wood tipped in a heap measures roughly a third more than it does stacked, because you are also measuring the air between the pieces. Always ask which one a quote refers to, because the difference is big enough to change which seller is actually cheaper.

faqs.q: How can I tell whether firewood is properly seasoned?
faqs.a: Seasoned wood is noticeably lighter than it looks, shows checking cracks across the end grain, and knocks together with a sharp rather than a dull sound. Wood that hisses at the cut ends while burning still holds water, which wastes heat and builds creosote in the flue.

faqs.q: Does a firewood seller have to tell me the volume?
faqs.a: In both New South Wales and Victoria firewood is sold by volume, and a seller should be able to state the quantity and provide a receipt showing it. A seller who will not give you a volume has answered the question of whether to buy from them. There are also rules on where commercial firewood may be sourced, so it is fair to ask.
